statement: Eight students are split into four pairs to work on a project. Only who is paired with whom matters. In how many different ways can the pairs be formed?

choices.misconception: I counted the ways to choose 4 of the 8 students to be the first person in each pair.
I divided by 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 instead of by 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24.
I divided by 4, the number of pairs, instead of by the 24 orders of the four pairs.
I chose a first pair, then a second, third and fourth, and did not allow for the order of the pairs.

hints: Choosing pairs one at a time gives them an order.
Count the ways to pick a first pair, then a second, and so on. That count treats the same four pairs in a different order as different, so work out how many orders four pairs have and divide by it.
Pair by pair gives 28 x 15 x 6 x 1 = 2520, and four pairs can be listed in 24 orders.

solutions.reliable: Choose a first pair from 8 students in 8 x 7 / 2 = 28 ways, a second from the remaining 6 in 15 ways, a third from 4 in 6 ways, and the last pair in 1 way: 28 x 15 x 6 = 2520. But the same set of four pairs is produced in 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 24 different orders, so there are 2520 / 24 = 105 ways. The transferable idea: when a count builds in an order that does not matter, divide by the number of orders.
solutions.elegant: Build each pairing in exactly one way: the first student has 7 possible partners, the first student still unpaired then has 5, the next has 3, and the last two are paired. So 7 x 5 x 3 x 1 = 105, with no overcount to correct.

whyOnTest: Overcount-and-correct: choosing pairs one by one secretly orders them, and the right divisor is the number of orders of the four pairs.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
